paragraphs.text: Today the ascension of the Savior has opened heaven to us and shown us the way of truth. Today the Savior's loving dispensation has drawn earthly man up from the earth and transplanted him into heaven. Today the goodness of the Only-begotten has snatched that old Adam out of the ancient condemnation, Adam who had been subjected to death, to the tomb and to lawless punishment. It has clothed him with immortality and set him in the very palaces of eternal life. And man on earth has become a fellow citizen of the angels; more than that, he has been shown to be master of the archangels and of all the heavenly powers. For the Savior's ascension does not merely rival the angels; it rules over them. For he is "far above all rule and authority and dominion and every name that is named," according to the saving teaching of the apostle, "who sat down," he says, "at the right hand of the Majesty on high." When the theologian says this, he is not describing the glory that he has had before the ages; he is setting forth the change of this mortal human race for the better. For it is not the Only-begotten, God the Word, coeternal and co-enthroned with the Father, who is taken up on high, since he is master of the things on high. It is mortal nature that is taken up by him. He does not procure salvation for himself; he bestows it on the human race. For he did not die for his own sake, nor rise for his own sake, nor was he taken up for his own sake. The fountain of immortality did not die, nor was the resurrection raised. God does not rise; he raises. He is not awakened; he awakens. He is not made alive; he makes alive. And so that you may learn that it is not God the Word who rises but the incarnate dispensation: before he endured the cross, before the burial, before he showed the resurrection, he said to Martha the sister of Lazarus, "I am the resurrection." He calls himself the resurrection to show that he raises according to his divinity but is raised according to his humanity. He rose, then, for our sake, since he also died for our sake. He was taken up into heaven, not because he himself needed heaven, he who fills heaven and earth, but in order to take the earthly vessel up into heaven. He did it to show the devil the one he had trampled now reigning, and to show that the one whom the devil's tyranny cast out of paradise, God's love for mankind has made to share its throne. God all but said to the devil's envy: "You wounded him on earth; I have caught him up into heaven. You brought him down into tombs; I have established him in my heaven." For, brothers, the Savior did not procure this salvation for himself, nor was he taken up for his own sake, nor did he ascend for his own sake. For he was in the world even before he came to dwell in the world. He endured all these things for us. In his own body he led us all up, and in the honor of sharing the throne that was given to the Savior's flesh we have all been honored and the mortal race has been glorified. Hear Paul saying: "When we were dead in our trespasses, he made us alive together with Christ, and raised us up with him, and seated us with him." He raised us up with him; why did he also seat us with him? You see that the honor was not given to himself, the fountain of immortality, but to the mortal race. He raised us up with him and seated us with him, and yet we have not yet been taken up, nor yet been seated with him. But since the salvation of all of us is stored up in Christ, the firstfruits of the body, he described what is to come as though it had already happened, because he knows that a secure pledge of the mortal race is seated on high. For God set the ascension as a counterweight against the fall into death. Adam, by transgressing, dragged the whole race down with himself; Christ, by being taken up, brought the whole race of the faithful up with himself. The sentence was pronounced against Adam alone, as it says, "On the day you eat, you shall surely die," and "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." What followed from it God left unsaid in words but showed in experience. For he did not say "you and your sons and your daughters and your whole race." By passing sentence on the root, he included the succession of the race, the fruits, along with the root. Just as the sentence on Adam there laid hold of the whole race and dragged it down, so the Savior's ascension procured salvation for the whole race. For grace is a counterweight to the old condition. I did not call it a counterweight as though the two were of equal worth. I called it so because what man lost through the transgression he received through the Savior's dispensation. And Paul bears witness, saying: "As in Adam we all die, so in Christ we shall all be made alive." Let no one wonder if, after the Savior had come, proclaimed eternal life and granted the kingdom of heaven, this mortal race disbelieved, saying: "What more have I gained by believing, if I come to my end like the unbelievers, if I am put to death along with everyone, if I endure the same things as those who disbelieved? What is new about grace? Where am I to find what is false and what is true?" Hear the Savior saying: "He who believes in me shall live forever." It was said to Adam, "On the day you eat, you shall surely die." But he did not die on the day he ate. He lived on in the world, yet he had already been made dead by the sentence. By the sentence he was dead, but by God's long-suffering he lived and enjoyed life. Adam's life was extended after the sentence to nine hundred and thirty years, and yet this did not annul the sentence; the sentence overtook him, having [?] the man's life over long years. So it is here too. Since he who made the promise is truthful once and for all, even if we die by nature, we live by the truthful promise. Living after the sentence did not set aside Adam's condemnation; in the same way, dying after the promise does not set aside our case. And our race has come to be in the lump according to the promise made from the beginning. It has received the benefit, and we are in heaven through Christ. Since we had come to be in tombs because of Adam, because of Adam we were cast out of paradise; through Christ we have been caught up both into heaven and into paradise. Because of Adam's transgression we were driven away by the cherubim. For it is written that God set the flaming sword and the cherubim to guard the way to paradise, and the cherubim were at war with Adam; they barred him from the entrance to paradise. Because of the transgression the cherubim are hostile to Adam; because of the Savior's promise the cherubim are friends and the seraphim fellow ministers. For the Church sends up the cry of the seraphim and the Thrice-Holy together with those above. It does so in order that man may learn that the heavenly powers were not at war with him by nature. They turned away from him because of his transgression and received him back because of God's love for mankind. There a flaming sword shut Adam out. But we are again taught that it was not the nature of fire that was at war with man; it was the transgression that set everything at war with him. A flaming sword drives Adam away; a chariot of fire takes Elijah up. Do you see how the same fire is both enemy and friend, not changing its nature but serving the purpose of God? Adam was shut out of paradise; Peter receives the keys of heaven. In paradise man is plotted against by the serpent. In the world, though handed over to exile, he tramples, in the very place of his exile, the one who trampled him: "For behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." Was it not the transgression that told against Adam? Then neither will the world tell against us, when faith justifies us. Adam in paradise is put to shame by his transgression; Job on the dunghill is crowned for his endurance. The lover of mankind, then, took up the human race: not one nation, not one region, but the whole inhabited world. For the fashioner of the whole human race saves the whole of man. All were fashioned in one way, and all share one calling. He does not allow the children of the Jews to pride themselves. See what he arranges even before his coming: he takes up Enoch. Which Enoch? The one who bears the type of the Church's good order. Why does Enoch become a type of the Church? Because he did not keep the Sabbath, did not receive circumcision and did not follow the Jewish observances; he was schooled in virtue by the simplicity of the gospel. So the firstfruits of salvation shone out beforehand. We had all passed sentence on our race as being mortal by nature, and out of ignorance all were ready to say that we die by nature, for custom had made the sentence pass for nature. So God took one man from that very lump and transferred him to immortality, to show that it was not nature that condemned them but sin that wounded them. He would not have overthrown the tyrant in any other way than by enduring the cross. By the tyrant I mean the devil, who played the tyrant over the Master's creation. For there are three things that reign in the world and tyrannize over the Master's handiwork. What are they? The devil, sin and death. For sin came through the devil, and death through sin. And where is it shown that these reigned? Scripture says: "Let not sin reign in your mortal flesh." And the same Scripture elsewhere: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned." There you have the reign of sin and of death. Hear the Lord saying: "If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand?" A triad of tyrants was arming itself against the immortal Trinity; a diabolical triad was set against the Holy Trinity. "Behold, the ruler of this world has been judged." Why did he say "has been judged" and not "has been destroyed"? Because he did not cast him out by force but by judgment. Pay close attention. God could have granted immortality to the mortal human race without the dispensation, without the cross, without the death of the flesh. For who will resist the will of God, whether his grace or his sentence? But as we have often said before, God provides for man not salvation only, but salvation with honor. He does this so that he may not seem simply to pity man, with no contest, but to crown him as one who has proved himself. For if the devil had been defeated by divine power, the tyrant would have thought great things of himself and would have said: "I conquered the whole world, and was defeated only by God; and there is no shame in being defeated by one who is stronger." For this reason the Savior raises up against him, as his opponent, the very man who had been overcome. The one whom the devil's tyranny brought down to the lowest depths of Hades, God has lifted up to the highest heights of heaven. And this is the resurrection of the Savior: the resurrection of us all, the dispensation for us all. Christ is proclaimed, and the world is set free from evils. Whatever Christ does, he does not provide for himself but bestows on us. He may be baptized for us; he may be sanctified, as far as appearances go. Yet he who sanctifies all is sanctified for our sake. He does not receive sanctification from some other power but supplies it to himself, bestowing the things of the Godhead on mortal nature, on human flesh. And he himself bears witness, saying: "For their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth." What does it mean to be sanctified in truth? It means to receive from the Savior's flesh the pledge of security. That is, to be sanctified in truth is to share in the Savior's divinity, to receive the Spirit from him and to give him the body. And see how grace begins from something small and advances into an ocean. When God begins to do good, he shows drops of his kindness: from a drop comes a spring, from a spring a river, from a river a boundless sea, from the sea a great deep. So the Savior appeared first and alone when he was about to renew the human race; he appears alone, not as one among many. From the one he advanced to twelve apostles, from the twelve apostles to seventy heralds, from the seventy heralds to five hundred brothers. For, it says, the Lord, when he had risen, appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once. From the five hundred, four thousand are caught in the net by Peter's preaching. At another of his teachings five thousand believed. It advanced from hundreds to thousands, from thousands to tens of thousands, from tens of thousands to a number beyond measure. In Jerusalem they say to Paul: "You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of Jews there are who have believed." Do you see how from one came twelve; from the twelve, seventy; from the seventy, five hundred; from the five hundred, thousands; from thousands, tens of thousands; from tens of thousands, a boundless multitude? So virtue seems small at its beginnings, but as it advances it gives an eternal wealth to those who piously proclaim the truth, a wealth surpassing thought and speech and reckoning. So too blessed David, once he had set his mind to it, takes it upon himself to number the friends of God, and shows his longing and declares that the task is endless, saying: "But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their dominions are greatly strengthened. I will count them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand." The growth seen in this church also bears witness to this dispensation. Consider what the assembly of orthodoxy in this place is: how few they once were, how afterward they became a multitude, how it grew and became a people, how countless tens of thousands now surpass both reckoning and imagination. It is fitting to remember the holy father Paul, who was bishop of this city, when amid many storms he moored the ship in a calm harbor. Though battered by the waves of heresy, the ship did not capsize. Raising the mast of the cross and spreading the sail of the good confession, it at once received the Holy Spirit. Let what was said of Abraham through Isaiah the prophet be said of him: "Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you in travail, for he was one, and I sanctified him and multiplied his seed." Who could bear the storms of the heretics? Who could look upon the tempest with the naked eye? Whom did the prevailing prejudice not bring to shuddering? Who did not think the truth something foreign? Everything had been opened to error and false teaching, and to truth alone everything had been shut. The gates of hearing were shut. No one opened the true door. For the ears are the doors that receive the truth, and when the ears turn away from the truth they shut it out like doors, as Paul says: "They will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths." The gates of souls were shut, the hearing of souls. Christ came while the doors were shut. He came in; he entered though the doors were shut. For not one evil can shut out his kindness. God's love for mankind conquers wickedness. He permits evils, not so that they may conquer but so that they may be exposed. He entered though the doors were shut. He showed himself to the apostles through the saints, and, visible through the flesh, he [?]. He found the whole people leprous and cleansed them by the word of orthodoxy. He found them blind and enlightened them by the word of teaching. He found them limping in the right handling of the gospel and granted them sound feet of reasoning. He found the dead and raised them. He found the lost and sought them out. He drove out unbelief by changing it into faith. For God's aim is to destroy not sinners but sin, to cut off not unbelievers but unbelief. A physician may apply the knife to a sick man, he may apply the cautery, yet he is not fighting the body; he is making war on the disease. When the disease has been banished, the man who resented him becomes his friend, and the one who once looked on the physician as an enemy afterwards honors him as a benefactor. So it is with God and humanity. He is like a good physician, healer of bodies and physician of souls: his treatment is one, his love for mankind, but he applies different medicines to the wounds. You know that a physician too does not take up the knife by his own choice. When nature is fighting the disease, necessity calls for sharp measures, and those who watch see that the art does not cut by its own choice but is driven to it by necessity. In this way the prophets also healed. They wished to soothe, to do good and to instruct, but when they saw that the wounds of sins were stronger than the art... I mean the art of faith at its height... they applied the reproof of truth like a knife or fire. So too blessed Isaiah fights the disease from the very outset. He does not cajole, he does not flatter, he does not use a gentle word; he begins at once with stern and austere truth, saying: "The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw against Judah and against Jerusalem." And this is how his opening begins: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood me. Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, evil seed, lawless sons." He used these words, cut away impiety from the outset and did not flatter the sinful soul with a gentle word. Then he defends what he has said, explaining that he is not provoked by choice but follows the nature of the wound, and he says to them: "There is no oil to apply, nor poultice, nor bandages." "I wanted to soothe you with a gentle word," he says, "but the nature of the wound does not admit that kind of help." For everywhere he calls gentle teaching "oil": teaching that has a soothing quality, not servile flattery but encouragement. The apostle too knows how to instruct the Church with a bright and gentle word, saying: "My little children, with whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you," and "As a nurse cherishes her own children, so, yearning for you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel but also our own souls." These are the words not of flatterers but of men adapting themselves to the holy body. Since he was addressing the healthy body of the Church, he no longer used harsh medicines but those that nourish and restore the soul. The speech of the ungodly, on the other hand, is full of flattery: the false prophets are flatterers, the prophets are physicians. The former flattered; the latter healed. And just as among bodies oil by nature rises above water, so vice prevails over truth, and the flatterer looks loftier than the one whose intent is to instruct. That is why David said of the false prophets: "Their words were softer than oil, yet they are darts." But the speech of the saints is not flattering but instructive. Hence blessed David chooses to be disciplined rather than flattered by the ungodly: "Let the righteous man discipline me in mercy and reprove me, but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head." Such was blessed Paul: he did not flatter but taught the truth. For it he suffers, for it he is exiled, for it he is crowned. This church has become for us the firstfruits of good things. God raised this church up first and made it namesake of his own resurrection. Fittingly the name matched the dispensation. Fittingly it was called Anastasis, the Resurrection, and let it be so called. Let her never leave off the contest, she who wounded false doctrine and raised up orthodoxy. She has raised up our souls; you, raise up her walls. Fit together her stones, so that she may fit together your souls. Raise up all her beauty, so that the benefit may be repaid in full. I rejoice to see the pledge of your zeal. Even if what has been offered is small for now, I know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump. Think of the altar as Christ's right hand stretched out, which to the eye receives but in power bestows. Christ's right hand is a spiritual field. It does not disappoint hopes, it does not waste the farmers' labors, it does not destroy their hopes. Christ's hand is a field sown at once and reaped at once. Do you want to see it as a field sown and reaped at the same time, receiving not only living seeds but dead ones too, and making them alive? In the wilderness five loaves were brought to Christ, loaves dead by the nature of the grain. For a grain of wheat is alive, but bread has undergone a twofold death: first when it is ground, and second when it is given to the fire. The loving right hand takes it and brings the dead thing to life. The Master's fingers spread over the loaves like furrows. His right hand receives the bread, blesses it and multiplies it beyond all thought. Do you see his right hand, a holy field? Do you see the loaves being sown? Do you see the word bedewing them, so that what was dead by nature is multiplied and what was barren by nature springs to life in countless thousands, not denying its nature but serving the divine power? Where Christ is present, do not look for the law of nature; look at the sovereign authority of the Mighty One. For he handed down the law of nature to you, but he himself, the Master of all, is above laws. For you there is rain, for you the spring, for you the years, for you the turning of the seasons; but none of these applies to the Craftsman. And as today the growth of these things has a twofold cycle [?]... First the infant is carried in the womb, then it is born, nursed and grows, and is brought to full manhood. But when God fashioned Adam, he needed no human seed, no womb, no pregnancy; when he willed it, he brought man forth. So he took the loaves, blessed them, multiplied them, broke them, gave them and fed the people. And see the marvel. When we invite people to a banquet, we first prepare what is needed and then invite them; we first make everything ready and then have them recline. But Christ first has them recline and then makes ready. He did not first increase the bread and then have them sit down. He first had them sit down and then bestowed the benefit, to show that his power is swifter than need. It was bread, and he multiplied it, not by its flowing away but by multiplying it without limit. It is not as the heretics imagine about God when they say, "If he begot by emanation and division, he was diminished." The bread did not flow away as it increased; what was dead was brought to life. Is the nature that gives life to all things then subject to laws of servitude? I follow your reasoning: tell me how the loaves increased, and then explain how God begot. In any case, the loving right hand took up the bread like seed. It multiplied it, broke it and gave it, and the hand was a treasury of good things. Looking to this right hand of the Savior, David said: "The eyes of all hope in you, and you give them their food in due season; you open your hand and fill every living thing with your good pleasure." ... [?] in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might and honor and worship, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
